title: What Is an Apicoectomy (Root-End Surgery)?
metaTitle: What Is an Apicoectomy? Root-End Surgery Explained
metaDescription: An apicoectomy is minor root-end surgery used when a root canal or retreatment is not enough. Learn what it involves and why it is often referred, in Markham.
excerpt: An apicoectomy is minor root-end surgery considered when conventional root canal treatment is not enough. Here is what it involves and why it is often referred.
heroImageAlt: Illustration of root-end surgery showing the tip of a tooth root being treated and sealed.
bodyHtml:
An apicoectomy, also called root-end surgery, is a minor surgical procedure in which the very tip of a tooth's root and any surrounding infected tissue are removed, and the end of the root is sealed. It is usually considered when a conventional root canal or retreatment has not resolved a persistent infection and the tooth is still worth saving. It is a specialised procedure, so it is often carried out by, or referred to, a dentist or endodontist with surgical training.

Where an apicoectomy fits in

Most infected teeth are treated successfully with a standard root canal, which cleans the canals from the top of the tooth. If a problem returns, the usual next step is non-surgical retreatment — reopening the tooth and re-cleaning the canals. An apicoectomy is generally reserved for situations where working through the crown of the tooth is not enough: for example, when infection or inflammation lingers at the root tip despite good canal treatment, or when the root anatomy makes a conventional approach difficult.

Thinking of it as a step in a sequence helps: root canal first, retreatment next where appropriate, and surgery such as an apicoectomy considered when those have not settled the problem and the tooth is a good candidate to keep.

What the procedure generally involves

Although details vary, an apicoectomy commonly includes these stages under local anaesthetic:

  1. The gum near the tooth is gently lifted to reach the bone over the root tip.
  2. The infected tissue around the root end is removed, along with a small portion of the root tip.
  3. The end of the root canal is cleaned and sealed with a small filling.
  4. The gum is placed back and secured with a few stitches while it heals.

The procedure itself is usually relatively short, though the exact time depends on the tooth and its position in the mouth. Recovery is generally straightforward, with some swelling or tenderness for a few days that is typically managed with standard aftercare advice — such as rest, cold compresses, and avoiding disturbing the area — from the treating clinician. Stitches are often removed or dissolve within a week or two. Your dentist or surgeon will give instructions specific to your case, and will usually plan a follow-up to check that the area is healing as expected.

Why it is often a referral

Root-end surgery calls for particular surgical skills and sometimes specialised equipment such as magnification. For that reason, a general or family dentist may assess the tooth, explain that an apicoectomy could be an option, and refer you to a clinician who performs this type of surgery. Being referred is a normal part of coordinated dental care and does not mean anything is wrong — it means the right person is matched to the procedure. If you want to understand how surgery fits alongside other options, your dentist can walk you through endodontic (root canal) care at Smile Dental Arts Centre and when onward referral might be suggested.

Is an apicoectomy the same as a root canal?

No. A root canal cleans the canals from the top of the tooth; an apicoectomy is a small surgery that treats the root tip from the side, usually after other approaches have been tried.

Does an apicoectomy save the tooth?

Its purpose is to keep a natural tooth that might otherwise be lost. Outcomes are generally good for suitable teeth, but no procedure can be guaranteed, and your clinician will discuss the specific outlook.

Will I be awake during it?

It is typically done under local anaesthetic so the area is numb while you remain awake. Options for comfort can be discussed with the treating clinic.

Next steps

If you have ongoing symptoms from a previously treated tooth, the first move is an assessment to find out why, and to see whether retreatment, surgery, or another option is most appropriate. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, can evaluate the tooth and discuss the path forward — including referral where surgery is indicated — at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
